a combination of clinical characteristics, environmental exposures, biomarkers of inflammation and genetic information can be combined in a risk prediction model to predict the course (persistence vs. remission) of childhood asthma.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

no single risk factor is sufficiently accurate to predict course of childhood asthma, and that the combination of several factors, including genetic information, may be more accurate than any single risk factor.
the evidence for predicting the course of early childhood asthma is limited and that further research is required to identify the most important predictors of persistence and remission.

the evidence to date suggests that the risk for persistent asthma is increased by the presence of early allergic sensitization, recurrent wheezing in the first years of life, and a family history of atopy and/or asthma, and that genetic factors also play a role.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is evidence that the course of early childhood asthma can be predicted, but that the predictive power of current tools is limited.
there is no simple way of predicting the course of asthma in young children.
the field is moving toward a better understanding of the factors that predict the course of asthma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of clinical, environmental, and biomarker data, and polygenic risk scores, could be used to predict the course and prognosis of asthma in early childhood.
the course of childhood wheezing is complex, but can be predicted to some degree by the use of a combination of clinical, environmental, and genetic information.
the prediction of the course of childhood wheezing is a priority for clinicians, families and researchers.
